newsitem.title: JAPAN: Albright arrives in Japan for Okinawa talks.
newsitem.headline: Albright arrives in Japan for Okinawa talks.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived in Tokyo on Sunday for a visit expected to be dominated by talks on the future of U.S. military bases in Japan.

Albright's visit coincides with leadership turmoil in North Korea, the unpredictable Stalinist state which is one of the main strategic reasons for the large American military presence in Japan, particularly on the southern island of Okinawa.
She arrived from the South Korean capital Seoul as part of a nine-nation tour, her first overseas visit since becoming secretary of state last month.
Albright has also visited London, Paris, Brussels, Rome, Bonn and Moscow. She leaves Tokyo on Monday morning for Beijing, the last stop on her tour.

Japanese officials have said food aid to North Korea, where the power structure is tottering with the departure in the past 10 days of three top officials, is a key issue that Albright will discuss with Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda.
The World Food Programme has estimated North Korea needs 2.3 million tonnes of grain this year to compensate for poor harvests as a result of devastating 1995 and 1996 floods.
But it appealed recently only for $41.5 million -- equal to 100,000 tonnes -- because that was all the U.N. agency felt it could raise from South Korea and other key states at this time.
Washington has pledged $10 million and Seoul $6 million.
Japan has held back so far from committing itself to new aid because of controversy at home over reports that agents from the communist nation have kidnapped Japanese citizens.

The reports, which have been denied by Pyongyang, said those kidnapped were put to work giving Japanese-language training to North Korean agents so that they could travel to carry out sabotage attacks.

The future of the U.S. bases on Okinawa has been threatened, just as tensions rise on the Korean peninsula, by the refusal of about 3,000 landowners to approve an extension of leases on the land occupied by the installations.
About 49,000 U.S. military personnel are based in Japan, more than half of them on the sub-tropical island 1,600 km (1,000 miles) southwest of Tokyo.
Okinawa hosts more than 75 percent of all U.S. military bases and Okinawans have long complained of noise, accidents and crime in areas near the sprawling military facilities.
The island is in easy striking range of North Korea, Taiwan and China.

An entire division of the U.S. Marine Corps is deployed on Okinawa. The breakdown of the 49,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan is 10 percent Army, 40 per cent Marines, and 25 percent each for Navy and Air Force.

Facing calls to cutback U.S. bases in Japan, Tokyo and Washington argue that a strong U.S. presence on strategically-located Okinawa is necessary to maintain stability in a potentially volatile region.
During a visit to Tokyo last April, President Bill Clinton agreed to a 20 per cent cut in the size of the Okinawa bases but the pledge failed to dampen down opposition to their presence.
Okinawa governor Masahide Ota has demanded the phased removal of all bases by 2015.
Public outrage about the bases has grown since the September 1996 rape of a young Okinawa schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen who are serving up to 10 years jail each for the crime.
